1.title: a word for wishing well on people you don't like
1.hook: a word for wishing well on people you don't like
1.tomorrow: the whole first instruction: in, out
1.howItsDone: Many Buddhists practice metta by silently repeating short wishes, such as may you be safe, may you be well, may you be at ease, first for themselves and then outward to loved ones, strangers, difficult people and all beings; the Metta Sutta is chanted in monasteries and homes.

segments.voice: Think of someone you don't like. Not a villain. Just someone. The coworker who replies all. The neighbor with the leaf blower at seven on a Saturday. The relative who has opinions about your life at every holiday. You probably have a face already. Now imagine a practice, thousands of years old, where people sit quietly and wish that person well. On purpose. Not because they've forgiven anything, and not because the person deserves it. Just as training, the way you'd train a muscle. It sounds almost backwards. It's one of the oldest things the Buddha taught. Today, the word for it.
screen: `THINK OF SOMEONE YOU DON'T LIKE.` → `NOW WISH THEM WELL.` → `ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: Metta. It's a word in Pali, the old language the Buddha's teachings were kept in. It comes from mitta, a friend. So metta is friendliness. A wish for someone's good, the plain warm kind you'd feel for a friend, pointed at anyone at all. You may know its Sanskrit cousin, maitri, or the name Maitreya, the kind one, the Buddha many Buddhists say is still to come. There's a short teaching on metta that Buddhists in many countries still chant. It pictures a mother protecting her only child with her own life, and says to hold a heart like that toward every living being. Seen and unseen. Near and far. Born and not yet born. Every one. That's the size of it. And the Buddha's own verses put the reason bluntly. In Max Müller's old translation of the Dhammapada: "hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love—this is an old rule." An old rule. Not a new idea even then. How do people actually do it? Later teachers laid out a gentle order. Start with yourself, because it's hard to give what you've never felt. Then someone you love. Then someone neutral, the person who sells you coffee. Then, last and slowest, someone difficult. You don't pretend to like them. You just wish them what you'd want: to be safe, to be well, to be at ease. Here's the surprise. People who practice metta often say it changes them more than it changes anyone else. The grip loosens. The difficult person is still difficult. But you're carrying less of them around.

segments.voice: Here's the practice for day one, and it's small on purpose. One breath, with the bell. Bring back that face from a minute ago. You don't have to feel warm. Breathe in slowly. And on the way out, let a few words go toward them, out loud or just inside: may you be at ease. That's all. One breath of friendliness, pointed somewhere unusual.
Metta. Friendliness. A wish for anyone's good, even the people who make it hard. First word on your strand.

segments.voice: Your line to carry: may you be at ease. Once today, when someone annoys you, in traffic, in a meeting, in a group chat, say it inside, just once, and notice what happens in you. That's day one. You showed up. See you tomorrow.

2.title: the whole first instruction: in, out
2.hook: the whole first instruction: in, out
2.howItsDone: Many Buddhists begin meditation by sitting upright and simply paying attention to the natural breath as it comes in and goes out, in monasteries, meditation halls and at home, often for a set time marked by a bell.

segments.voice: Yesterday: metta, friendliness, from the word for a friend. Your line was may you be at ease. Did someone annoying get one quiet wish? Day two.

People imagine meditation is hard to start. You need a cushion, an app, incense, a retreat in the mountains, a mind that goes blank on command. Then you actually read how the Buddha is remembered teaching it, and the first instruction is almost funny in how small it is. Sit down. Breathe in, and know you're breathing in. Breathe out, and know you're breathing out. That's it. That's the doorway. And the one thing it needs, you've been doing all day without being asked, since the minute you were born. Today's word is the oldest meditation object there is.
screen: `NO CUSHION REQUIRED.` → `IN, AND KNOW IT.` → `OUT, AND KNOW IT.`

segments.voice: The breath. In the old Pali texts, the practice is called anapanasati: mindfulness of breathing in and breathing out. There's a whole discourse on it, and it begins with a scene. A monk goes to the forest, or the foot of a tree, or an empty room. He sits down, crosses his legs, keeps his body upright, and sets his attention right in front of him. Then, mindful, he breathes in. Mindful, he breathes out. Breathing a long breath, he knows it's long. Breathing a short breath, he knows it's short. Notice what's missing. Nobody tells him to breathe in a special way. No counting to four, no holding, no fixing. The breath is left exactly as it is. The job is only to know it. That's a quiet revolution, because most of us spend the day not knowing we're breathing at all. Why the breath? Teachers give a few reasons. It's always with you, so you can practice on a bus. It's always now; you can't breathe yesterday's breath. And it sits right on the line between what you do and what just happens, so watching it teaches you something about both. The discourse goes on for sixteen steps, from the breath to the body, to feelings, to the mind, to the deepest things the Buddha taught. But every one of those steps is still riding on the same in and out. Across Buddhist countries and schools, Zen, Tibetan, Theravada, the breath shows up again and again as a place to begin. Not because it's special. Because it's already here.

segments.voice: One breath, with the bell. Don't change anything. Don't make it deep or slow or impressive. Just let the next breath come in, and know it's coming in. Feel where it's easiest to notice: the nose, the chest, the belly. Then let it go out, and know it's going out. One whole breath, known from start to finish. That's the entire first instruction, done.
The breath. The first meditation object, always with you, always now. Breathing in, knowing it. Second word.
Your line: you're already doing it. Three times today, at a red light, in a line, before you open a message, notice one breath all the way through. Day two.

3.title: not "suffering"
3.hook: not "suffering" — the wobble in the wheel; the itch under everything
3.tomorrow: a rich kid who saw a sick man, an old man, a corpse, and a monk
3.howItsDone: Buddhists learn dukkha as the first of the four noble truths, and many teachers invite students simply to recognize it in daily life, the aches, the endings, the restlessness, without adding blame or panic.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the breath. In, and know it. Out, and know it. Your line was you're already doing it. Did you catch a breath at a red light? Day three.

You finally get the thing. The new phone, the weekend off, the apartment with the good light. And for a day or two it's wonderful. Then, very quietly, something starts to itch. The phone has a scratch. The weekend is already half over on Saturday night. The light is great, but the neighbors are loud. Nothing is wrong, exactly. It just doesn't quite sit right. There's a word for that. It's usually translated as suffering, and that's why so many people think Buddhism is gloomy. But the word is smaller and stranger than suffering. It's about a wheel.
screen: `YOU FINALLY GET THE THING.` → `THEN, QUIETLY, AN ITCH.` → `A WORD ABOUT A WHEEL.`

segments.voice: Dukkha. It's the first big word of the Buddha's teaching, and it's almost impossible to translate. Suffering is the usual choice. Some translators say stress, or unsatisfactoriness, which is accurate and nobody can say it twice. So teachers often reach for a picture instead. A popular explanation splits the word in two. Du, bad. Kha, a hole, and in particular the hole in the middle of a wheel, where the axle goes. A cart with a badly fitted wheel still rolls. You still get where you're going. But every turn has a little jolt in it. That's dukkha. Its opposite is sukha, a good axle hole, which came to mean happiness: a smooth ride. Scholars aren't sure that's where the word really comes from. But the picture has stuck because it fits. Buddhist teachers describe three layers of it. The first is plain pain: a toothache, a breakup, a funeral. Nobody needs that explained. The second is the pain of change: the good thing that's already ending while you're enjoying it, the Sunday evening feeling. The third is the subtlest: the low hum of everything being conditioned, dependent, never quite solid enough to rest on. The itch under everything. Here's why this matters, and why it isn't gloomy. The Buddha didn't point at dukkha to make people sad. He pointed at it the way a doctor names what's wrong, because naming it is the first step toward treating it. Recognizing the wobble is not the same as being crushed by it. Often it's a relief. Oh. It's not just me. It's the wheel.
screen: `DUKKHA — HARD TO TRANSLATE.` · `DU, BAD. KHA, THE AXLE HOLE.` · `PAIN, CHANGE, THE HUM UNDERNEATH.` · `NAMING IT IS THE FIRST STEP.` · then, large: `THE WOBBLE IN THE WHEEL.`

segments.voice: Three breaths, with the bell. On the first breath, notice one small wobble right now. A tight shoulder. A worry about later. A message you haven't answered. On the second breath, don't fix it. Just name it: this too. On the third breath, notice that the wobble and the breath are both here, and the breath is still coming in and going out.
Dukkha. Not only suffering: the wobble in the wheel, the itch under things, the ride that's never perfectly smooth. Third word.
Your line: this too. Today, when something small goes slightly wrong, the coffee's cold, the meeting runs long, just say inside, this too, and see if it wobbles a little less. Day three.

4.title: a rich kid who saw a sick man, an old man, a corpse, and a monk
4.hook: a rich kid who saw a sick man, an old man, a corpse, and a monk
4.howItsDone: Buddhists honor the Buddha as a teacher and example, bowing to his image, offering flowers, light and incense at shrines, and celebrating his birth, awakening and death, often together on the festival of Vesak.

segments.voice: Yesterday: dukkha, the wobble in the wheel. Your line was this too. Did something small go wrong, and did the words help? Day four.

Picture a prince in the foothills of the Himalayas, around two and a half thousand years ago. His father has given him everything. Palaces, music, fine clothes, and, the story says, a life kept carefully away from anything ugly. Then one day he goes out riding. By the road he sees an old man, bent over. Then a sick man. Then a dead body being carried to the fire. Then a wandering monk, owning nothing, and somehow calm. Four sights. He goes home and can't stop thinking about them. That rich kid is the person the whole path is named after.
screen: `A PRINCE WHO HAD EVERYTHING.` → `FOUR SIGHTS BY THE ROAD.` → `HE CAN'T STOP THINKING.`

segments.voice: Buddha isn't a name. It's a title. It comes from a Pali and Sanskrit root, budh, to wake up. A buddha is someone who has woken up. His name was Siddhattha, of the Gotama family, from the Sakya people, in the borderlands of what's now Nepal and India. Historians place him somewhere in the fifth or sixth century before the common era; the exact dates are argued about. The four sights you just heard are how later tellings of his life begin, and that's worth being honest about. The oldest discourses tell a very similar story about an earlier buddha, and the Buddha himself remembers his young life more plainly: a comfortable home, and a growing shock at aging, sickness and death. The four sights may be a story. The question inside them is real. Here's what that rich kid did with it. He left the palace, lived for years as a wandering seeker, nearly starved himself, gave that up, sat down under a tree, and woke up. Then he spent about forty-five years walking the roads of northern India, teaching anyone who would listen: kings, farmers, beggars, women, people from every caste. And here's the part that surprises people. In the oldest texts he never claims to be a god. When someone asks what he is, a god or a spirit or a man, the story goes that he answers simply: awake. Theravada Buddhists especially emphasize that he was a human being who found a way and showed it. Many Mahayana traditions also speak of the Buddha on a vaster, cosmic scale. But in every school, the story starts with a person.
screen: `BUDDHA — ONE WHO WOKE UP.` · `SIDDHATTHA GOTAMA, OF THE SAKYAS.` · `THE PALACE, THE ROAD, THE TREE.` · `NOT A GOD. AWAKE.` · then, large: `HE WAS A PERSON.`

segments.voice: Three breaths, with the bell. On the first, think of an old face you know. On the second, think of someone who is sick, or has been. On the third, think of the calmest person you've ever met. The same four sights he saw are all around you, all the time. For three breaths, let yourself see them, the way he did.
The Buddha. Not a name but a title: the one who woke up. A person who found a way, and spent his life showing it. Fourth word.
Your line: he was a person. Today, look at one statue, picture or image of the Buddha you pass, on a shelf, in a shop, online, and remember: a real human being started this. Day four.

5.title: there is dukkha
5.hook: there is dukkha; the relief of someone saying it
5.howItsDone: Buddhists learn the four noble truths as the heart of the Buddha's first teaching; the first sermon is remembered every year, and in Theravada countries its anniversary is marked on the full moon of Asalha.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Buddha, the one who woke up. Your line was he was a person. Did you pass an image of him and remember a real human started this? Day five.

You're at the doctor. Something's been off for weeks. You've googled it at two in the morning, you've told yourself it's nothing, you've told yourself it's everything. And then the doctor looks at the chart and says, calmly: yes, this is what it is. Strangely, you feel better. Nothing has been fixed yet. But someone has finally said it out loud, and said it plainly, and you're not imagining things. The first thing the Buddha taught after he woke up works a lot like that moment. Today, the first of four truths.
screen: `SOMETHING'S BEEN OFF FOR WEEKS.` → `THE DOCTOR SAYS WHAT IT IS.` → `STRANGELY, YOU FEEL BETTER.`

segments.voice: After his awakening, the story says, the Buddha walked to a deer park near the city of Benares, today's Varanasi, to find five old companions. His first teaching to them is remembered as setting the wheel of the teaching in motion. And the first thing he says, after warning them off two extremes, is four truths. They're called the noble truths, ariya sacca. Some scholars read that as the truths of the noble ones: the truths that someone who's awake can see. The first is short. There is dukkha. Then he lists it, and the list is ordinary. Birth is dukkha. Aging is dukkha. Sickness, death. Being stuck with what you don't like. Being separated from what you love. Not getting what you want. You could write that list yourself. That's the point. Here's what makes it a teaching and not a complaint. It's called a truth, not a verdict. It doesn't say life is bad. It doesn't say you're doing it wrong. It says: this is the situation, for everyone. Teachers have long compared the four truths to a doctor's visit. The first truth is the diagnosis. The second finds the cause. The third says it can be cured. The fourth is the treatment. You can't treat what nobody will name. And there's a detail in the text that people miss. The Buddha says this first truth is something to be understood. Not fixed, not escaped, not believed. Understood. Looked at clearly. Which is where the relief comes in. You're not uniquely broken. You're a human being, and the wheel wobbles for everyone.
screen: `THE DEER PARK. FIVE OLD FRIENDS.` · `THERE IS DUKKHA.` · `A DIAGNOSIS, NOT A VERDICT.` · `SOMETHING TO BE UNDERSTOOD.` · then, large: `IT'S NOT JUST YOU.`

segments.voice: Three breaths, with the bell. On the first, think of something that's been hard lately, whatever comes. On the second, picture how many other people, right now, in this city, in this country, are carrying something just like it. On the third, let that land. Not as a problem solved. As company.
The first noble truth. There is dukkha. A diagnosis, spoken plainly, to be understood. Fifth word.
Your line: it's not just you. Today, when someone tells you something is hard, don't rush to fix it. Say something plain, like, yes, that's hard. Day five.

6.title: craving
6.hook: craving — wanting things to be other than they are
6.howItsDone: Buddhists learn the second noble truth as the arising of dukkha from craving, and in meditation many practice noticing wanting and aversion as they come up, without acting on them right away.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the first noble truth. There is dukkha, a diagnosis, not a verdict. Your line was it's not just you. Did someone tell you something hard? Day six.

segments.voice: You're in a slow line at the grocery store. The person ahead is paying in coins. Counting them. Out loud. Notice what happens in your body. The jaw tightens. The weight shifts. A little voice starts narrating: why is this line always the slow one. Now here's the odd thing. The line is just a line. It isn't hurting you. What hurts, if you look closely, is the gap between the line that is and the line you want. That gap has a name. The Buddha said it's where the wobble comes from. Today, the second truth.
screen: `THE SLOW LINE.` → `THE JAW TIGHTENS.` → `THE GAP BETWEEN IS AND WANT.`

segments.voice: The second noble truth is about where dukkha comes from. In Pali it's samudaya, arising, origin. And the Buddha's answer is one word: tanha. It literally means thirst. Not a polite preference. Thirst. The dry-mouthed, leaning-forward kind that makes you reach before you think. In the first sermon he names three thirsts. The thirst for pleasant things: the next bite, the next scroll, the next thing to buy. The thirst to be something: to be seen, to be right, to last. And the thirst not to be: to make something go away, to disappear from a feeling, to wish this moment weren't happening. That third one surprises people. Even pushing away is a kind of craving. The line at the grocery store is thirst of that third kind. You want not to be in it. Here's a careful point. Buddhism doesn't say every wish is a problem. Teachers distinguish craving from other kinds of wanting: the wish to be kind, the intention to practice, the will to get up and help someone. Those have a different Pali word, chanda, and they're part of the path. What the second truth names is the grasping kind. The kind that insists: this should be different, right now, or I can't be okay. And here's why it's hopeful, not harsh. If the wobble came from the world, you'd be stuck. You can't make every line fast. But if the wobble comes from the thirst, then there's something you can actually work with. The thirst is closer to home.

segments.voice: Three breaths, with the bell. On the first, find something you want right now. Food, a message, for this lesson to end. Anything. On the second, feel where the wanting lives in your body: the chest, the hands, the jaw. On the third, don't get rid of it. Just notice that it's a feeling, and it's thirsty.
The second. The second noble truth: dukkha has an origin, and the origin is tanha, thirst, wanting things to be other than they are. Sixth word.
Your line: the wanting is the wobble. Today, next time you're stuck waiting, a line, a download, a slow reply, look for the thirst underneath it, and name it. Day six.

7.title: it can stop
7.howItsDone: Buddhists speak of nirvana as the end of craving and of dukkha; in Theravada it is the goal of the path, and many Mahayana traditions describe awakening in their own terms, while everyday practice keeps attention on letting go.

segments.voice: One week. Look at your strand. Metta, the wish for anyone's good. The breath, in and out. Dukkha, the wobble in the wheel. The Buddha, a person who woke up. The first truth: there is dukkha. The second: it comes from thirst. If the week ended there, it would be a pretty heavy week. A diagnosis and a cause. But the Buddha didn't stop at two, and neither do we. Think of the moment a headache you've had all day finally lifts. You didn't notice it arriving. You notice it leaving. Today, the truth that says the wobble can end.

segments.voice: The third noble truth is nirodha. Cessation. Stopping. In the first sermon it's put simply: when the thirst fades away completely, when it's let go and released, dukkha ends. Remove the cause, and what it causes stops. The name for that ending is one you've heard: nirvana, in Sanskrit, or nibbana, in Pali. It's built from a word for a flame going out. Blown out, the way a candle goes out when there's no more fuel. That's the image. Not a place you go. The fire of craving, with nothing left to burn. People sometimes hear that and think it sounds like nothingness. The texts don't describe it that way. The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's old translation, lists the best things there are: "Health is the greatest of gifts, contentment the best riches; trust is the best of relationships, Nirvana the highest happiness." Happiness. Not blankness. And there's a famous exchange in the discourses. A wanderer asks the Buddha where a fully awakened person goes after death. The Buddha asks him: when a fire goes out in front of you, which direction did it go? North? South? The man admits the question doesn't fit. The fire just went out. The Buddha says this question is like that one. Buddhists across traditions describe nirvana in different words, and the texts often prefer to say what it isn't. But the third truth itself is simple, and it's the hinge of everything. The wobble is real. And it isn't permanent. There is an end.

segments.voice: Three breaths, with the bell. On the first, notice any small wanting that's here. On the second, notice any small ache. On the third, notice a moment, even a flicker, where neither is pulling at you. A gap. A small quiet between two thoughts. It might be tiny. That tiny thing is what the third truth is pointing at.
The third. The third noble truth, nirodha: when the thirst ends, dukkha ends. The flame goes out. Seventh word, and a week done.

Your line: there is an end. Today, notice one ache or irritation actually ending, a pain easing, a worry passing, and pay attention to it leaving the way you'd pay attention to it arriving. Day seven.
